items.item: A page has five parts (header, line-pointer array, free space, items, special space), and item identifiers grow from one end while item data grows from the other, meeting in the middle.

at.out: planned: a reveal step drawing a real page's five parts

items.item: A line pointer (ItemIdData) is an (offset, length) pair, 4 bytes, that never moves once allocated until freed, even when the item it points to is physically relocated to compact free space.
A CTID (the row's visible identity) is a page number plus a line-pointer index, not a byte offset — this is exactly why a row's logical identity survives being moved within the page.

at.out: planned: the predict step and its reveal

items.item: The heap tuple header has a fixed size (23 bytes on most machines) followed by an optional null bitmap (one bit per column, present only if any column is null) before the real column data begins.

at.out: planned: a reveal step on a real inserted row with a null

items.item: A fixed page size (8 kB by default) is the direct cause of TOAST's existence: PostgreSQL tuples cannot span pages, so a value too large to fit is compressed and/or chunked into a separate TOAST table instead.
TOAST chunks a large value into roughly 2 kB pieces stored as separate rows in a side table (chunk_id, chunk_seq, chunk_data), triggered once a row crosses the 2 kB threshold.

InnoDB solves the identical fixed-page problem with its own overflow pages rather than a side table, and different row formats (COMPACT, DYNAMIC, COMPRESSED) store different amounts of data out of line.
pageinspect's get_raw_page and heap_page_items are the real, direct way to read a live page's own bytes rather than trust a diagram — this topic should use them on a real page, not simulate one.

at.out: planned: every reveal step, built from a real page read

items.item: A page checksum and the pd_lsn field exist so a torn or stale page can be detected — this connects directly to the next topic's own write-ahead-logging material and shouldn't be taught in depth here.
